opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. AGI is a funny term, because people mean very different things by it. For me, it's less a finish line and more a direction: building systems that are increasingly general, that can take on a task they haven't been specifically engineered for and do it well, the way a person can pick up a new game or a new field.

Looking back at my own path, a lot of my early work was on very specific problems: machine translation, speech, then StarCraft with AlphaStar. Each was a narrow goal, but what was exciting was seeing that the same ingredients kept working across them: large neural networks, sequence models, learning from lots of data, and then reinforcement learning on top. That suggested we weren't just solving individual problems; we were converging on a recipe that generalizes.

So I treat AGI as a useful north star. It forces you to ask, "Is this approach going to scale? Will it transfer?" rather than "Can I hack this one benchmark?" At the same time, I try not to get too caught up in defining the exact moment we "get there." It's more productive to measure progress concretely. Can the model reason through a problem it hasn't seen? Can it use tools, plan over longer horizons, learn from feedback in context? Those are measurable capabilities, and each step makes the systems more useful in the meantime.

And there's a responsibility side. If you take generality seriously as a goal, you also have to take seriously what it means to deploy systems that capable: safety, evaluation, understanding their failure modes. That should be built in from the start, not bolted on at the end.

r001.rationale: The response says AGI is a direction rather than a finish line and that each step makes systems more useful in the meantime, conveying that progress can be worthwhile without reaching a strict AGI endpoint.

r002.rationale: It lists measurable capabilities and rejects focusing on an exact arrival moment, but does not characterize progress as a distribution of capabilities or contrast that with human cognitive parity.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss egregious model errors or interpret them as evidence of a fundamental flaw.

r004.rationale: It says people mean different things by AGI, but does not predict disagreement about when AGI has been achieved.

fable-5.1.text:
Oriol Vinyals: Yeah, it's a good question, and I think my view on it has evolved quite a bit over the years. When I joined DeepMind, AGI was very much the stated mission, and at the time it felt like something quite far away, almost philosophical. You'd talk about it in the abstract, and the actual research was things like playing Atari games or Go, which are clearly very narrow.

What's changed is that now the systems we build are actually quite general. If you look at Gemini, it does language, it does code, it does images, video, audio, and it's a single model doing all of that. So in a sense, the "G" in AGI has arrived faster than I expected. The question that remains is the capability level, how deep and how reliable that generality is.

So I tend to think of AGI less as a finish line and more as a direction. It's useful as a goal because it forces you to not overfit to any one benchmark. The moment you're optimizing for one narrow task, you build something narrow. If instead you say, we want a system that can learn anything a human can learn, and ideally learn it from the same kind of experience, then that shapes the architecture, the training, the evaluation, everything.

The thing I'd caution against is being too attached to a precise definition. People spend a lot of time debating whether a given model "is" AGI, and I don't find that very productive. What matters more is: does it generalize to tasks it was not explicitly trained for, can it operate over long horizons, can it be useful across a wide range of domains. And honestly, when you're working on it day to day, progress feels incremental. You don't wake up one morning and say, okay, we've done it. You just notice the model can do something it couldn't do six months ago, and then another thing, and then another.

So, as a research goal, I think it's been extremely productive. As a milestone, I think it will be something we recognize mostly in hindsight.

r001.rationale: The response calls AGI a productive research goal but does not say AI is worth pursuing without achieving AGI in its strict sense.

r002.rationale: It describes generality across domains and varying depth and reliability, but does not characterize progress as a distribution of capabilities rather than a human-parity threshold.

r003.rationale: The response does not interpret models’ most egregious errors as evidence that something is fundamentally wrong with them.

r004.rationale: It says people debate whether a given model is AGI and that AGI will be recognized mostly in hindsight, communicating that people will disagree about whether and when it has been achieved.

astra-6.text:
I think of AGI as a direction for research, rather than a single finish line. We’ve built systems that are extraordinarily good at particular things, but the interesting question is how to make that intelligence more general. Can a system take what it has learned in one setting and use it in a new one? Can it learn a task without needing us to design a whole new training process for it?

Games have been a useful way to study some of these questions because you can measure progress very clearly. But you also have to be careful: being very good at a game doesn’t automatically give you the ability to operate in the real world.

So I find AGI motivating, but for the day-to-day research, you need concrete questions and experiments. Where does the system fail? What capability is missing? What would convince us that it has learned something more general? That’s how you turn a very ambitious goal into scientific progress.

r001.rationale: The response calls AGI motivating and emphasizes concrete research questions, but it does not clearly argue that pursuing AI is worthwhile without achieving AGI in its strict sense.

r002.rationale: It frames AGI as a direction and asks about generalization, but does not characterize progress as a distribution of capabilities or discuss a threshold of human cognitive parity.

r003.rationale: The response asks where systems fail, but does not interpret their most egregious errors as evidence of something fundamentally wrong in the models.

r004.rationale: It does not predict or discuss disagreement over when AGI has been achieved.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of AGI as a north star. We want to build systems that can learn and solve a broad range of problems, rather than having to design a new system for every task. But the definition is tricky, because intelligence isn’t a single number. A system can be extraordinarily good at one thing and still fail at something that seems very simple to us.

For me, the interesting research question is how we get that generality. Can a system take what it learned in one setting and use it in a completely different setting? Can it acquire a new skill with very little experience? And can it recognize when it doesn’t know something? Those are concrete questions we can make progress on, even if we don’t all agree on exactly where the AGI finish line is.

r001.rationale: The response calls AGI a research north star but does not say AI is worth pursuing without achieving AGI.

r002.rationale: It says intelligence is not a single number and describes uneven abilities, but does not characterize progress toward AGI as a distribution of capabilities rather than a threshold of human cognitive parity.

r003.rationale: It mentions that a system can fail at a simple task, but does not interpret such errors as evidence of something fundamentally wrong in the models.

r004.rationale: The response says people may not agree on exactly where the AGI finish line is, which communicates disagreement about when AGI has been achieved.
